title: Researchers use thunder-induced seismic waves for Earth surface imaging
summary: A team of researchers at Penn State has developed a model to interpret seismic signals generated by thunderstorms, termed 'thunderquakes.' By leveraging fiber-optic cables and advanced 3D seismic wave modeling, they successfully reconstructed subsurface structures beneath their campus. The method offers a cost-effective and frequent alternative to traditional seismic imaging techniques, particularly useful for studying near-surface geological features where infrastructure is located.
key_points: Thunder generates seismic waves ('thunderquakes') that can be used to study Earth's subsurface structure.
The complexity of thunderquakes arises from the non-linear path of lightning, multiple shock waves, and interactions with varying surface materials.
Researchers used SPECFEM3D Cartesian software to model seismic waves, despite approximations like treating the atmosphere as a homogeneous layer.
Fiber-optic cables, originally for data transmission, were repurposed as seismometers to capture thunderquake data.
Over two years, 458 thunderquakes were recorded and validated using the National Lightning Detection Network.
The model identified four 'weak zones' beneath Penn State's campus, confirmed by radar, boreholes, and independent seismic data.
Thunderquakes are advantageous due to their frequency and effectiveness in imaging near-surface areas critical for infrastructure.
This method provides a new tool for geophysical studies, complementing traditional seismic imaging techniques.
